items.title: L12: Leadership at SEO
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: At SEO level, Leadership usually shifts from leading a team to leading an area, often through other managers. Typical evidence is setting a direction that other leaders carry out, building a leadership culture, leading people through uncertainty, and challenging practice that others have accepted. At HEO a good answer shows how you motivated the people you supervise. At SEO the assessor often wants to see how you led people you do not directly manage, and how you made leaders beneath you effective. Examples include leading a programme board of peers, setting the tone for a division after a damaging report, or steering a merger of two teams with different working cultures. Scope is a typical test: how many people, how many teams, and how far did your influence reach? Independence is the second test: did you decide the direction, or follow a plan someone else wrote? Strong answers describe a specific moment of leadership, such as telling staff an uncomfortable truth about a funding cut, and what you did next to keep people engaged. Weak answers describe a post or a list of responsibilities. Another common weakness is leading only by authority: an SEO who says 'I told the managers what to do' has described control, not leadership. Inclusion matters at this level too, for example making sure that quieter voices influence decisions and that opportunities are fairly shared. Be honest about difficulties; a leadership story with no setbacks can seem implausible. State clearly what changed because of your leadership, such as improved engagement, a restructure that held, or a decision that stuck.

questions.prompt: Which description of SEO-level Leadership fits the general pattern best?

options.text: Motivating and supporting the individuals you personally supervise, and checking their work day to day
Setting a direction that other managers carry out and making those managers effective
Following a leadership plan written by a senior colleague
Completing management training and applying the standard model

questions.hint: Scope through other leaders marks the grade.

questions.prompt: A candidate writes 'I told the managers what to do and they did it.' How would an assessor most likely read this?

options.text: As strong leadership, because the managers did what was asked and the result was delivered on time
As control rather than leadership, with nothing on motivating or involving others
As evidence of inclusive leadership
As evidence of Delivering at Pace instead

questions.hint: Leading only by authority is weak.

questions.prompt: Which is the clearest sign of independence in a Leadership example?

options.text: You consulted your manager and sponsor before each step and recorded their agreement
You attended every meeting about the work
You received positive feedback from the sponsor
You decided the direction instead of implementing a plan someone else wrote

questions.hint: Independence is whether you set the direction.

questions.prompt: Which moment would make the most convincing SEO leadership evidence?

options.text: Telling a division about a funding cut honestly and then agreeing with its managers how to protect priorities
Circulating a director's email about the funding cut with a short covering note of reassurance to all staff in the division
Waiting until the cut was announced publicly before speaking to staff
Asking each manager to explain the cut to their own team

questions.hint: A specific uncomfortable moment and what followed.

questions.prompt: Why might a leadership story with no setbacks seem implausible?

options.text: Real leadership through change almost always meets difficulties, and honesty about them builds credibility
Setbacks are required in every example by the marking scheme, so a story without one is automatically scored lower
Assessors prefer stories about failed projects
A story without setbacks is too short to score

questions.prompt: Which question tests scope in a Leadership example?

options.text: How many people and teams were affected, and how far did your influence reach?
How long did you spend preparing the plan, and how many drafts did it go through before approval?
Who approved the plan?
How many meetings did you chair?

questions.prompt: Leading a programme board of peers is useful SEO evidence mainly because it shows what?

options.text: Chairing meetings that run to time and keeping accurate records of the actions agreed
Leading without formal authority by gaining the support of equals
Reading complex papers quickly
Holding a more senior post than the other members

questions.prompt: Which result most clearly shows leadership effect after a merger of two teams?

options.text: The merger plan was approved by the board after two rounds of comments from the sponsors and the unions
The merged team kept working to the agreed model a year later and staff survey results held up
The merger was announced on schedule
Both team leaders attended the first joint meeting

questions.hint: Durability of the change is the real result.

questions.prompt: Which action best shows inclusive leadership at SEO level?

options.text: Using the same meeting pattern for every group so that nobody could claim to be treated differently
Making sure quieter voices and part-time staff shaped a decision and shared in new opportunities
Asking the most experienced staff to speak first and last
Taking decisions only with those present on site

questions.hint: Inclusion includes fair influence and opportunity.

questions.prompt: How should an SEO describe credit for a team's success?

options.text: Say the team succeeded because of their direction and that nobody else made a significant contribution
Leave out their own part to avoid claiming credit
State what they personally did to enable it and what the team did
Credit the sponsor with the whole result

items.title: L12: Making Effective Decisions and Big Picture at SEO
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: For Making Effective Decisions at SEO, assessors usually look for decisions with significant consequences, taken under uncertainty and with competing pressures such as cost, risk, public reaction and political context. The decision is often one that others cannot easily reverse, or one where there is no precedent. Strong answers show a structured approach: clarify the question, gather evidence of differing quality, take expert and stakeholder advice, test the assumptions, weigh the options against criteria, decide, explain the reasoning transparently and review. A senior decision-maker should also show how they handled the limits of their authority, for example by deciding what to take to a minister or board and what to settle themselves. Seeing the Big Picture at SEO normally looks further ahead and wider afield than at HEO: anticipating how policy, technology, funding or public expectations may shift, and shaping the team's contribution accordingly. Evidence might include scanning for trends, building scenarios, or adjusting a long-term plan before a crisis. A frequent weakness at both Behaviours is describing the outcome but not the reasoning. Another is a decision where the candidate only recommended, with someone else deciding; say whether you recommended or decided. Also avoid describing a decision made with perfect information, since senior decisions seldom have it. Value for money, fairness and the interests of future users are all legitimate considerations, and mentioning them shows breadth. Where the decision was later shown to be wrong, say what you did. Review and learning are part of the Behaviour at every grade.

questions.prompt: Which feature makes a decision example more suited to SEO than HEO?

options.text: Significant consequences, hard to reverse, taken under uncertainty and competing pressures
A short deadline, a well-defined set of options and a manager available to make the choice with you
A single stakeholder who agreed with the result
A decision made inside the candidate's own team

questions.hint: SEO decisions carry weight and ambiguity.

questions.prompt: Where a candidate only recommended and someone else decided, what should the statement do?

options.text: Describe it as the candidate's decision for clarity, since the recommendation was followed in full
Leave out the decision-maker
Present the recommendation as a joint decision
State plainly that it was a recommendation and what the candidate's part was

questions.hint: Honesty about the role in the decision.

questions.prompt: Which element best reflects handling the limits of authority?

options.text: Deciding what to take to a minister or board and what to settle yourself
Passing every difficult decision upwards so that no senior leader is ever surprised by an outcome
Making every decision without consulting anyone
Waiting until a more senior colleague returned from leave

questions.hint: Judging escalation is part of senior decision-making.

questions.prompt: A statement describes the outcome of a decision but not why that option was chosen. What is missing?

options.text: The date on which the decision took effect and the name of the person who signed it off
The names of those who attended meetings
The reasoning: criteria, evidence and the options weighed
The wording of the final announcement

questions.prompt: Which example best shows Seeing the Big Picture at SEO?

options.text: Reading the departmental business plan and sharing a summary with every member of the team
Adjusting a long-term plan early after scanning for shifts in funding and public expectations
Explaining the team's current priorities clearly
Responding quickly to an urgent ministerial request

questions.prompt: Why is a decision made with perfect information a poor choice of example?

options.text: Perfect information makes the decision too easy to explain and leaves the assessor nothing to probe at interview
Senior decisions seldom have complete information, so the story shows little judgement
Assessors dislike decisions that turned out well
It cannot be written within a word limit

questions.hint: Judgement under uncertainty is the test.

questions.prompt: Which consideration would show breadth in a public-sector decision?

options.text: The preference of the candidate's immediate manager and the sponsor of the work in question
The speed with which the candidate made the decision
The number of options the candidate could think of
Value for money, fairness and the interests of future users

questions.prompt: What is a reasonable way to show testing of assumptions?

options.text: Stating that the assumptions were correct because they had been used in earlier decisions
Listing every assumption without any checking
Describing how a key assumption was checked with data or experts before deciding
Asking a colleague to confirm the decision

questions.prompt: After a decision was later shown to be partly wrong, what would an assessor value most?

options.text: An explanation that the evidence available at the time was misleading and incomplete
What the candidate did to correct course and what was learned
A statement that the decision was the best available
A note that others agreed with the decision

questions.hint: Review and learning are part of the Behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which action best shows transparent explanation of a decision?

options.text: Telling the team the decision was final, to avoid reopening the discussion once it was made
Passing the decision to a manager to announce
Sending the decision with no reasoning to avoid argument
Setting out the options, criteria and reasoning in a paper available to those affected

questions.hint: Transparency gives affected people the reasoning.

items.title: L12: Changing and Improving at SEO
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: At SEO level, Changing and Improving usually involves leading change that reaches across a function or service, often supported by a business case, with benefits that are tracked after delivery. Where a HEO might redesign a process across two teams, an SEO is more likely to lead a programme that changes how a whole area works, bringing different groups and leaders along. Typical evidence includes building the case for change with data, winning backing from sponsors, designing the change to manage risks, making sure staff are prepared, and checking whether benefits were actually achieved. Strong SEO answers often show an understanding that change is a human process: people have different stakes, and resistance can be a source of useful information. They also show a willingness to stop or alter an approach that is not working. Innovation is welcome, but it is judged by outcomes and by whether risks were managed; a novel idea with no evidence of results scores less than a plain improvement that clearly worked. Digital and data are common contexts, but the Behaviour is not limited to technology. Typical weaknesses include describing a project you managed administratively without saying what you decided, claiming the benefits of a whole programme, and presenting a plan with no evidence it was implemented. Another is failing to mention what you stopped doing: sustainable change often means retiring old practices. Where the benefits were uncertain at the time of the application, say so and describe how they were being measured, rather than claiming them as achieved.

questions.prompt: Which feature most clearly separates SEO from HEO in Changing and Improving?

options.text: Suggesting changes to the working practice of a team and helping colleagues adopt them
Leading change across a function with a business case and tracked benefits
Applying a ready-made improvement method to one process
Joining a project group on a single new system

questions.prompt: Why can resistance be useful to a change leader?

options.text: It proves that the change is working, because only effective changes provoke a reaction
It shows that staff are unwilling to change and will need firmer direction
It can reveal real risks and gaps in the plan
It can be ignored once the sponsor approves

questions.prompt: Which of these is the weakest as evidence?

options.text: Describing a programme you administered without saying what you decided
Describing how you adjusted a plan after a pilot and agreed the changes with the sponsor
Describing how you secured sponsor backing
Describing how benefits were measured

questions.prompt: A novel idea with no evidence of results scores less than what?

options.text: A copy of another department's idea
An idea that the manager suggested and the candidate then developed into a plan
A plain improvement that clearly worked and was measured
A change that was approved by a board

questions.prompt: Why might an SEO mention what they stopped doing?

options.text: To reduce the number of words in the statement by leaving out the detail of the new approach
To show that the previous team was ineffective
Sustainable change often means retiring the old practices it replaces
To avoid claiming credit for the new approach

questions.prompt: The programme's benefits were not yet measurable at the time of application. What should the candidate do?

options.text: Claim the planned benefits as achieved, since the programme is due to deliver them shortly
Say so and explain how the benefits are being measured
Choose a different Behaviour
Leave out any mention of benefits

questions.prompt: Which claim is most likely to be challenged at interview?

options.text: Describing a pilot that was stopped early after the candidate's review of its first results
Explaining why a plan was changed after feedback
Naming a risk that materialised
Claiming the whole programme's benefits when the candidate led one workstream

questions.prompt: Which element helps show that staff were prepared for a change?

options.text: A single announcement on the day of launch, with the guidance placed on the intranet
Targeted briefings and support timed before the new process went live
A written note placed on the intranet
Waiting for staff to ask questions

questions.prompt: Which statement about the contexts for this Behaviour is accurate?

options.text: Only technology and digital change count as evidence at SEO and above
Process, service and cultural change count as well as technology
Only change formally approved as a programme with a business case counts
Only change that reduced cost counts, whatever its effect on the service

questions.hint: The Behaviour is wider than technology.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best shows building a case for change?

options.text: Data showing the problem, options appraised, sponsor backing, then design
Sponsor instruction, design, rollout, thanks to the programme team and a closing report
An idea, a poster, a pilot, a celebration
A complaint, an apology, a new form, closure

items.title: L12: Communicating and Influencing at SEO
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: At SEO level, Communicating and Influencing typically involves persuading senior and sometimes external audiences, including ministers' offices, boards, partners and the public, often on contested or sensitive matters. The audience may be sceptical, senior to you or has competing interests, and your influence may be limited to the strength of your case and your credibility. Strong answers show that the candidate prepared by understanding what each party cared about, shaped the message and its channel accordingly, anticipated challenge, and judged when to compromise. Examples include securing funding at a spending round, negotiating a shared service with another department, briefing a minister's private office on a risky issue, or handling difficult press or stakeholder reaction. Honesty matters: Civil servants are expected to give full and accurate information, and a good answer shows balance and a willingness to bring bad news early. The Civil Service Code also requires political impartiality, so evidence about influencing ministers should show advice given fairly and without a personal political stance. Weak answers describe presenting information to a senior group with no sign of influence, or a campaign of communications measured only by outputs such as the number of emails sent. A stronger measure is a change in behaviour or a decision. At SEO the assessor often wants evidence of influence upward and sideways, not only downward through the line. Describing a written submission or a negotiation in terms of its objective, your approach and the result gives the most useful evidence. Name the compromise you made, where relevant, since it shows judgement.

questions.prompt: Which audience type is most typical of SEO-level Communicating and Influencing?

options.text: Senior, sceptical or external audiences with competing interests
Colleagues in your own team who share your view and meet you every day
A single manager who has asked for the work
Staff who report directly to you

questions.hint: SEO influence is upward, sideways and external.

questions.prompt: Which element of preparation would an assessor most expect?

options.text: Writing the longest and most detailed briefing possible so that no point was missed
Practising your presentation until it was memorised
Understanding what each party cared about and anticipating their challenge
Taking a colleague with you for support

questions.prompt: Why does the Civil Service Code matter in evidence about advising ministers?

options.text: Ministers must always be agreed with once they have taken a decision, whatever the evidence
Advice must be limited to written briefings
Ministers should not be told bad news
Advice should be given fairly and impartially, without a personal political stance

questions.prompt: Which is a stronger measure of influence than the number of emails sent?

options.text: The number of recipients on the circulation list and the number who opened the message
The length of the communication plan
A change in a decision or in what people did as a result
The speed with which the plan was written

questions.prompt: A candidate presented information to a board but nothing changed and nothing was asked of it. What is missing?

options.text: A longer presentation with more slides and a fuller account of the background to the issue
The names of the board members
A statement that the candidate was nervous
A purpose of influence, such as a decision or action the candidate sought

questions.prompt: Why should a candidate name a compromise they made?

options.text: It shows that the candidate lost the argument and had to accept the other side's position
It increases the word count
It shows that others disagreed
It shows judgement about what to concede to reach agreement

questions.prompt: Which statement shows bringing bad news early?

options.text: I waited until the report was complete so that I could explain the delay and its cause in full
I mentioned the delay only if asked
I asked my manager to decide whether to tell them
I told the private office about the delay as soon as I knew, with options for how to handle it

questions.prompt: Which example would be considered influence upward?

options.text: Training a new starter on the case system and checking their work during the first month
Briefing your team on a policy change
Updating a colleague on progress
Persuading a director to change a funding allocation using evidence

questions.prompt: What should a written submission example state?

options.text: Its objective, your approach and what happened as a result
The number of pages, the date and the grade of the person who cleared it
The title of the submission and the sponsor
That the submission was cleared

questions.prompt: Why is a campaign measured only by outputs weak?

options.text: Outputs show activity but not whether anyone was persuaded
Outputs are not allowed in applications because they cannot be checked by assessors
Campaigns cannot be measured
Outputs are difficult to count

items.title: L12: Working Together at SEO
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: At SEO level, Working Together generally means building and sustaining partnerships that deliver outcomes no single team could, often across departments, with external bodies, or between groups with real conflicts of interest. Typical evidence includes brokering an agreement between departments about shared responsibilities, creating a joint team with a clear shared goal, working with a delivery partner or supplier in a way that respects both sides' constraints, or resolving a long-standing dispute about who owns a service. The focus moves from being a good collaborator to creating the conditions for others to collaborate. Strong answers show the candidate understood each party's incentives, created a shared purpose, set clear roles, dealt with disagreement directly and kept the relationship in good repair. They should also show that the candidate shared credit and did not push the cost of the arrangement onto others. Diversity and inclusion remain central: building partnerships that include different communities, voices and ways of working is expected, for example by consulting groups affected by a service. A recurring weakness is describing a governance structure, such as a board or terms of reference, without saying how people were brought to use it. Another is a partnership in which everything went smoothly, which gives no sign of how conflict was handled. Be careful to separate this Behaviour from Communicating and Influencing: if the answer is about winning an argument, it belongs there; if it is about the joint working arrangement and the trust built, it belongs here. Identify your personal contribution in a multi-party project, because assessors need to see what you did.

questions.prompt: What shift marks Working Together at SEO rather than HEO?

options.text: From working with colleagues to working more independently on your own projects and tasks
From being a good collaborator to creating conditions in which others collaborate
From attending meetings to chairing them
From internal contacts to a wider social network

questions.prompt: Which action best shows understanding of each party's incentives?

options.text: Offering the same terms to every partner so that nobody can say they were treated differently
Presenting your own department's needs first
Asking what each organisation needed from the arrangement before proposing roles
Asking the sponsor to decide the terms

questions.prompt: Describing a governance structure with no sign of use is weak because what is missing?

options.text: A diagram of the structure showing the reporting lines between each of the boards
Evidence of how people were brought to work within it
The names of the board members
A note on the meeting schedule

questions.prompt: A partnership story where everything went smoothly has what weakness?

options.text: It shows nothing about how conflict was handled
It suggests that the candidate was inactive and that others did the work of the partnership
It means the example is too recent
It shows the candidate worked alone

questions.prompt: Which example fits Working Together rather than Communicating and Influencing?

options.text: Persuading a director to approve funding for the work after a series of difficult meetings
Setting up a joint team between two departments with shared goals and clear roles
Presenting a case to a minister
Writing a persuasive submission

questions.prompt: Which action reflects sharing credit?

options.text: Presenting the result as your department's alone so that responsibility for it is clear
Leaving out partners to simplify the account
Naming partner contributions in the final report and at the launch
Thanking the partners by email afterwards only

questions.prompt: Which of these shows inclusion in a partnership?

options.text: Consulting groups affected by the service on the design of the joint arrangement
Limiting membership to the senior staff of each partner to keep decisions quick and accountable
Setting meeting times to suit the lead department
Using a single feedback form

questions.prompt: How should a candidate treat a multi-party project in a statement?

options.text: Identify their own contribution amid the contributions of others
Claim the project as theirs, since they were the person who brought the partners together
Describe only the project's results
Describe the partners' roles only

questions.prompt: Which approach best respects a supplier's constraints?

options.text: Setting the most demanding timetable possible so that the supplier has an incentive to prioritise the work
Leaving the supplier to raise any concerns
Waiving any contractual checks
Agreeing deliverables that fit their capacity and being open about your own limits

questions.prompt: Which step helps keep a relationship in good repair after a dispute?

options.text: Reviewing what went wrong together and agreeing what will change
Closing the issue without further discussion so that both sides can move on to the next task
Asking each party to record their view separately
Escalating to a senior leader at once

items.title: L12: Developing Self and Others at SEO
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: At SEO level, Developing Self and Others usually extends to building the capability of an area, not only individuals. Typical evidence includes managing performance fairly across managers, building a pipeline of future leaders, creating an environment where people can learn from mistakes, using data on skills and diversity to guide action, and supporting managers to have difficult conversations. Developing yourself continues: strong SEO answers show honest self-awareness, such as seeking feedback from people who report to you, acting on it, and learning from outside the Civil Service. Assessors often look at how you developed other leaders, since SEOs are expected to multiply their effect. For example, an SEO who coaches a HEO to run a difficult restructure and then steps back develops capability that outlasts the SEO's involvement. Succession planning, mentoring across grades, and building inclusive routes into leadership for under-represented groups are all relevant. Care is needed in the handling of performance: a good example shows fair, evidence-based, timely action that respects the individual's dignity and the rules. Confidential details should not be exposed. Weaknesses include describing a training programme the SEO commissioned but did not shape, claiming development of staff who simply performed well, and focusing only on high performers. A balanced answer shows attention to people at different points: those who are struggling, those who are strong and those who are new. The best evidence includes some follow-up showing that the development took hold, such as a person who went on to lead independently, or a team that now solves problems it used to escalate.

questions.prompt: What marks the SEO expectation in Developing Self and Others?

options.text: Completing your own personal development plan on time and recording it for the annual review
Attending more training than colleagues
Managing the learning budget
Building the capability of an area, including other leaders, not only individuals

questions.prompt: Which example best shows developing another leader?

options.text: Coaching a HEO to run a difficult restructure, then stepping back so they lead independently
Sending a HEO on a recognised leadership course, then recording their attendance and sharing the course feedback with them
Taking over the HEO's restructure to finish it faster
Writing the HEO's objectives on their behalf

questions.prompt: What is the main weakness of describing a training programme you commissioned but did not shape?

options.text: Programmes are not accepted as evidence in written statements at any grade
It suggests the candidate had a large budget
It is too long
It does not show the candidate's own actions in developing people

questions.prompt: Which answer shows balance in developing people?

options.text: Concentration on the highest performers, who are most likely to progress to senior roles
Concentration on staff nearing a promotion board
Concentration on staff with the longest service
Attention to struggling, strong and new colleagues, each with tailored support

questions.prompt: Why is a follow-up outcome valuable evidence?

options.text: It proves the training budget was spent well and that the approach should be repeated
It shows that the candidate monitors attendance
It shows the development took hold, for example someone leading independently
It confirms the HR record

questions.prompt: Which self-development example is strongest?

options.text: Reading widely about leadership in your own time and applying some of the ideas you found
Completing a qualification relevant to the post
Asking people who report to you for feedback, acting on it and checking again later
Receiving a good annual rating

questions.prompt: A good performance example at SEO level would show what?

options.text: Quick removal of the person from the team once the concerns had been put to them
Fair, evidence-based and timely action that respected the person's dignity
Informal comments with no records
Leaving the matter to the line manager

questions.prompt: What should be done with confidential personal details in the answer?

options.text: Include full details so that the assessor can verify what happened and who was involved
Omit the example entirely
Describe the situation in general terms and focus on your actions
Share details only with the panel chair

questions.prompt: Which describes building a pipeline of future leaders?

options.text: Identifying potential, giving stretch roles and sponsoring people from under-represented groups
Promoting staff with the longest service first, since they have the most experience of the work
Keeping top performers in their current roles
Hiring externally for every vacancy

questions.prompt: A team that now solves problems it used to escalate shows what?

options.text: That the manager is less involved in the day-to-day work of the team than before
That fewer decisions are made
That the team is more senior
Capability that has been built and will outlast the leader's involvement

items.title: L12: Managing a Quality Service and Delivering at Pace at SEO
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: At SEO level, Managing a Quality Service typically concerns the quality, risk and assurance of a whole service, often with a budget, a supplier chain and public accountability. Assessors usually look for how you set the standard, how you obtain assurance that it is met, how you handle risk and how you respond when something fails publicly. Examples include overseeing the recovery of a service after an audit finding, setting up performance measures that tell the truth, and managing complaints and parliamentary or media scrutiny. Good answers show that the candidate used management information carefully and did not let a favourable headline hide a poor underlying picture. Delivering at Pace at SEO usually concerns a portfolio or programme: balancing several demands, allocating scarce resources, managing dependencies and keeping delivery confidence honest. A key test is whether the candidate made trade-offs and communicated them, for example agreeing with a sponsor to defer a lower-priority deliverable to protect a critical one. Pace without quality is a weakness in both Behaviours, as is quality without any regard to cost and timeliness. Typical weaknesses include describing a service without a standard or measure, claiming delivery success with no evidence of the risks managed, and showing heroics rather than systems. Reporting to a senior board with honest confidence ratings, such as admitting a project is at risk, is stronger evidence than a series of green statuses. Where costs are sensitive, describe scale in general terms. Say what you decided, and what you left to others.

questions.prompt: What generally marks Managing a Quality Service at SEO?

options.text: Checking the work of a small team and acting on the errors found in it each week
Following a standard set by a manager
Responsibility for quality, risk and assurance of a whole service under public accountability
Answering complaints in your own team

questions.prompt: Which use of management information shows good judgement?

options.text: Reporting the headline figure to the board with a short note on the trend since last year
Using only the measures that the supplier provided
Looking beneath a favourable headline to find where performance was weak
Comparing this month with the last month only

questions.hint: Do not let headlines hide poor detail.

questions.prompt: What does honest delivery confidence involve?

options.text: Reporting every project as on track until there is clear evidence that it has failed
Telling the board when a project is at risk, with the reasons and options
Waiting until a project has failed to report it
Reporting only to the sponsor

questions.prompt: Which action shows a sensible trade-off at SEO?

options.text: Asking the team to work longer hours on everything until every deliverable has been completed
Dropping the critical deliverable to meet the date
Delaying the whole programme
Agreeing with the sponsor to defer a lower-priority deliverable to protect a critical one

questions.prompt: Why are heroics weaker evidence than systems?

options.text: Heroics are against Civil Service rules on working time and are never accepted as evidence
Systems are cheaper than people
Heroics depend on one person's effort, while systems keep working without them
Heroics take more time to explain

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest quality example at SEO?

options.text: Passing an audit with no findings and receiving a letter of thanks from the auditors
Maintaining the existing standard
Setting up performance measures that exposed hidden problems and then acting on them
Reporting results as required

questions.prompt: What is the issue with 'delivery was successful' with no further detail?

options.text: It is too short for a statement
It repeats the Behaviour wording instead of giving any facts for the assessors to score
It shows the candidate did not manage the work
It gives no risks, trade-offs or measure for assessors to score

questions.prompt: When something fails publicly, what would assessors value?

options.text: Explaining that the failure was outside your control and caused by an external supplier
Waiting for the press to lose interest
Taking responsibility, being open about causes and fixing the root problem
Handing the matter to another team

questions.prompt: Why is quality without regard to cost or timeliness a weakness?

options.text: Cost is the only measure of quality that the public and Parliament are interested in
Timeliness is not part of quality
Assessors prefer the cheapest option
Public services have to deliver value for money and on time, as well as to standard

questions.prompt: How should sensitive cost figures be handled in a statement?

options.text: Describe the scale in general terms that you can defend at interview
Leave out any mention of scale, as the figures are confidential to the department
Give exact budget codes
Round the figure upward

items.title: L12: Which example best shows a Behaviour at a given grade?
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: A common task, in sifts and in preparation, is to compare examples and judge which fits a Behaviour at a particular grade. A reliable method uses five questions. First, is the Behaviour actually shown? Look for its characteristic verbs: decided, improved, led, influenced, delivered. If the central action is another one, the example fits another Behaviour. Second, is the scope right for the grade? An example that affects one desk is likely to be too junior for HEO; one that sets direction for a function is typical of SEO. Third, is the candidate's own part clear? A larger scope is no help if the reader cannot tell who did what. Fourth, is there a result? Evidence without outcome is weak. Fifth, is it credible? Specific, balanced detail, including difficulties, signals a real example. Applying the questions often shows that the more impressive story is not the best. A big programme described in general terms, with the candidate's role unclear, may lose to a smaller episode in which the candidate's judgement is visible. At the same time, a very small example for a senior role is still a risk, so the aim is the best fit, not the smallest or the largest. When two examples fit, consider breadth across the application: choosing the story that is least duplicated elsewhere strengthens the whole. Always read the advert's description of the Behaviour at the stated level, since it names the scope expected. Assessors may also look for balance between success and learning: an example that shows how you responded to something going wrong can score well if the learning is clear. The best examples are often recent and verifiable, in case an interviewer probes.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the first question to ask of a candidate example?

options.text: Is it the most dramatic and memorable example available to the candidate?
Was it completed this year?
Does it actually show the characteristic action of the Behaviour?
Does it involve a senior person?

questions.prompt: Why might the more impressive story lose to a smaller one?

options.text: Impressive stories are always rejected because assessors suspect them of being exaggerated
Small stories always score higher
Assessors prefer shorter examples
The big story may leave the candidate's own part and reasoning unclear

questions.prompt: A very small example for a senior role is a risk because what is missing?

options.text: A named result and a measure of its effect
Any use of the STAR structure at all
Any reference to the Behaviour by name
Scope that matches the grade expected

questions.prompt: When two examples fit equally, which is the better choice?

options.text: The one with the most numbers and the largest budget attached to it
The one that involved the most colleagues
The one not duplicated elsewhere in the application
The one that happened most recently

questions.prompt: Example X: 'I led a programme that transformed services', with no detail of actions. Example Y: 'I decided to pause a rollout after a pilot showed errors, explained this to the sponsor and redesigned the test.' For Making Effective Decisions, which is better?

options.text: X, because the scale is bigger and the programme sounds more senior
X, because it mentions leadership and uses the language of the profile
Both equal, because both are about work delivered
Y, because the decision, reasoning and action are visible

questions.prompt: Which feature of the advert should shape the choice of example?

options.text: The closing date and the number of examples that applicants are asked to provide
Its wording of the Behaviour at this level, including the scope expected
The salary band, the working pattern and the civil service grade of the post
The location of the post and the name of the hiring manager named in it

questions.prompt: Example A: ‘I redesigned a form that my team used.’ Example B: ‘I redesigned an application process used by three teams, piloted it and cut errors, though one pilot step failed and was changed.’ For Changing and Improving at HEO, which is stronger?

options.text: B, because of scope, measured result and honest difficulty
A, because it is simpler to explain and clearly the candidate's own work
A, because it is clearly the candidate's own and carries no risk of overclaiming
Both equal, because both are redesigns

questions.prompt: Why does credible detail include difficulties?

options.text: Real work involves problems, so a story without them looks less believable
Assessors score each difficulty mentioned as extra evidence towards the Behaviour
Difficulties make the answer longer
Difficulties demonstrate bad planning

questions.prompt: Which candidate answer shows an example fitting another Behaviour than the one asked?

options.text: A Working Together answer on building joint working across two departments with a shared goal
A Working Together answer on resolving a long-standing conflict between two partner teams
A Working Together question answered mainly by describing persuading a director to agree a plan
A Working Together answer on including remote and part-time staff in the project team

questions.hint: Persuasion belongs to Communicating and Influencing.

questions.prompt: Why prefer recent, verifiable examples?

options.text: Older examples are not allowed under any circumstances in a Civil Service application
Recent examples are always larger
Interviewers may probe, and recent facts are easier to defend accurately
Assessors do not read old examples

items.title: L12: Spotting too-junior wording in a senior draft
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: A draft statement can fail for a senior post simply because its language and structure describe work at a lower grade. Several cues are worth checking. Look at verbs. Phrases such as 'assisted', 'supported', 'helped', 'was asked to' and 'was involved in' usually suggest a contributor rather than an owner. For an SEO example, stronger verbs often include 'decided', 'sponsored', 'negotiated', 'commissioned', 'challenged' and 'led', provided they are true. Look at who set the agenda: if a manager always set the direction, the independence expected at senior grade is missing. Look at the audience: a draft whose only audiences are the candidate's own team or manager is probably pitched low. Look at the scale: single cases, single customers and single tasks may be fine for a lower grade but typically need to widen to teams, services or whole processes. Look at risk: senior answers usually deal with risks and consequences, not just completion. Finally, look at the result: 'the task was completed' is a junior result, whereas 'the service met its target and the approach was adopted elsewhere' shows wider effect. Rewriting is not a matter of replacing verbs: if the facts do not support the stronger verb, the example should be replaced, since overclaiming is a serious risk. If the underlying work is solid but modestly pitched, the fix is often to bring forward the decisions and judgement you actually exercised and to show their consequences, rather than inventing scale. Try reading each sentence and asking 'who decided this?' and 'who else was affected?'. Where the answer is always 'my manager' and 'nobody', the example is too junior.

questions.prompt: Which phrase is the strongest signal of a contributor rather than an owner?

options.text: I decided to pause the project
I was asked to help with the project
I sponsored the change
I negotiated the terms

questions.prompt: A draft's only audiences are the candidate and their manager. What is the likely issue?

options.text: It is too long for a sift and repeats the same point about the manager
It uses too many figures
It is pitched low, with too little breadth of audience for a senior role
It describes too many people

questions.prompt: A draft replaces 'helped' with 'led', but the facts show the candidate was an assistant. What is the problem?

options.text: The stronger verb is not supported by the facts, which is overclaiming
The verb is too short to convey the full scope of what the candidate did
The draft now has too many verbs
The verb must match the manager's

questions.prompt: What is the better fix for solid work that is modestly pitched?

options.text: Add larger numbers so that the scale of the work looks closer to the grade
Bring forward the real decisions and judgement and show their consequences
Add more adjectives
Change the example to a different team

questions.hint: Surface the truth rather than inflate.

questions.prompt: Which result suggests wider effect?

options.text: The task was completed to the standard that was expected by the sponsor
The service met its target and the approach was adopted by another team
The manager was satisfied and gave the candidate positive written feedback
The deadline was met in spite of a shortage of staff in the team

questions.prompt: Which question helps reveal a junior draft?

options.text: How long is the draft compared with the word limit set in the advert?
Which verbs are used most frequently in each paragraph of the draft?
How many paragraphs are there and how many words does each use?
Who decided this, and who else was affected?

questions.prompt: A draft contains no risks, only completion of tasks. What does this suggest?

options.text: The example is probably pitched below senior level
The example is too risky for a senior role and should be replaced
The example has a good result and a clear completion date
The example is well structured and follows the STAR format

questions.prompt: Which description is the most senior?

options.text: I helped to gather the data for the review and supported the sponsor throughout the whole process
I attended every review meeting and supported the people who gave evidence to the reviewers
I was involved in the review from the first meeting until the report was published
I commissioned an independent review, challenged its findings and changed the service model

questions.prompt: Which scale cue suggests a lower-grade example?

options.text: A service used by many customers across several regions of the country
A process crossing several teams and a number of suppliers
Single cases or single tasks with no wider pattern
A decision affecting a function

questions.prompt: Why is it not enough to replace verbs only?

options.text: Verbs are not marked by assessors, who read only for results
Seniority comes from the substance of decisions, scope and consequences, not word choice
Assessors read only the opening sentence of each paragraph in the statement
Verbs reduce the word count and so should be kept to a minimum in every sentence

items.title: L12: Leading through others without losing your own part
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Senior roles act mainly through other people, which creates a difficulty for written evidence. If your managers delivered the result, how can the statement show what you did? The answer is to describe your leadership actions precisely: what direction you set, what you asked of others, what support you gave, how you checked progress and what you did when things went wrong. Verbs matter here. 'I set the objective that every complaint would be answered within five working days, agreed measures with the three team leaders, and met each weekly to review progress' is clear about your part. 'My teams reduced complaints' is not, since it credits others and conceals you. Equally, 'I reduced complaints' hides the managers who did the work and is likely to be probed. The honest middle is to name the roles: 'my three team leaders redesigned the case checks; I challenged the first design, which was too slow, and agreed the final one'. A reader can then see your judgement and the delegated work. Delegation itself is evidence of leadership if it was thoughtful: matching tasks to people, giving the authority needed and offering support. Decisions you took not to intervene can also be described, because holding back is often a leadership choice. Be careful about counting the success of an entire directorate as your own. State the part that was yours, such as the direction, the key decision, the escalation, or the relationship you managed. If you have to describe many contributors, use a single sentence for them and spend the rest of the words on your own actions.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best shows your own part while leading through others?

options.text: My teams reduced complaints by about a quarter within the first six months of the year
Complaints fell steadily under my leadership and the directorate hit its overall target
I set the objective, agreed measures with the three team leaders and met each weekly to review progress
The directorate achieved its target after a period of sustained effort by all of the staff

questions.prompt: Why is 'My teams reduced complaints' weak?

options.text: It credits others and conceals what the candidate did
It is too specific about the outcome and so cannot be checked
It mentions complaints, which are not a suitable subject for a Behaviour statement
It uses the word teams, which assessors read as describing the wrong grade

questions.prompt: What is the risk of 'I reduced complaints' when others did the work?

options.text: It is too short to give assessors enough of the story to score
It overclaims and is likely to be probed at interview
It uses the first person, which statements at this grade should avoid
It suggests a manager did nothing while the candidate carried the team

questions.prompt: Which wording is the honest middle?

options.text: The case checks were redesigned and the new version was adopted across the service
My three team leaders redesigned the case checks; I challenged the first design and agreed the final one
I redesigned the case checks myself and then asked my team leaders to adopt them
We redesigned the case checks together as a leadership team and agreed the final version

questions.prompt: How can delegation count as evidence?

options.text: If it reduced your own workload and freed time for more strategic work
If it was thoughtful: matching tasks to people, giving authority and offering support
If it was recorded in a formal plan and approved by the sponsor
If it covered all tasks, so that nothing was left to the leader

questions.prompt: Why might a decision not to intervene be worth describing?

options.text: It shows the candidate was absent from the work and avoided taking responsibility
It avoids describing risks that the candidate would otherwise have to own
Holding back can be a leadership choice that lets others learn and own the result
It shows the candidate was unconcerned about the outcome for the team

questions.prompt: When many people contributed, how should the words be used?

options.text: Equal space for each person, to be fair to everyone who took part
A list of every contributor with a note of each one's task
One sentence for the contributors and the rest on your own actions
Focus entirely on the outcome and leave the contributors to the sponsor

questions.prompt: Which of these is a part of your own that could be stated?

options.text: The team's achievements during the year, as recorded in its annual report
The sponsor's praise for the way the programme was delivered
The key decision, the escalation or the relationship you managed
The work plan and the timetable that the team followed

questions.prompt: Which action best shows how you checked progress through managers?

options.text: Reading the final report and asking the managers to explain any differences from the original plan
Asking the sponsor to monitor the work and tell you immediately if it was falling behind
Trusting that the work was done well because the managers were experienced and reliable
Agreeing measures with them and reviewing results regularly, stepping in if data slipped

questions.prompt: Counting a whole directorate's success as your own is risky because what?

options.text: It is not allowed in Success Profiles guidance for any grade of post
It is likely to be challenged and weakens credibility
It always lowers the score of the example by one band
It shows the directorate was weak and needed the candidate's direction

items.title: L12: Inflated, vague or buzzword evidence
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Senior drafts are prone to a particular kind of vagueness: inflated language that sounds strategic but names nothing. Phrases such as 'drove transformation', 'leveraged stakeholders', 'delivered at scale', 'shaped the agenda' or 'embedded a culture of excellence' feel senior but give an assessor no facts to score. A useful test is to ask whether the sentence could appear in anyone's application. If so, it is not evidence. To fix it, replace each abstraction with a specific: which stakeholders, what was asked of them, how many people, what changed, and how you know. Instead of 'embedded a culture of excellence', write what you did, for example 'introduced a monthly review where each team presented its three most frequent errors and the actions it had taken; within a year, the repeat error rate fell by about a third'. Be cautious with statistics. Figures must be true and defensible, and you may be asked how they were calculated. A vague claim of 'significant savings' is weaker than an honest 'around a tenth of the annual running cost'. Another version of vagueness is the long list of responsibilities: an SEO who sets out the whole portfolio has described the job but not an action. Choose one or two moments within it. Also avoid unexplained acronyms and internal programme names. Assessors may sit in another department and cannot score what they cannot understand. Finally, keep sentences plain: long chains of nouns and passive verbs hide who acted. A senior statement written in clear English signals confidence and makes it easier for the assessor to give credit.

questions.prompt: Which test identifies buzzword evidence?

options.text: Is the sentence longer than the average sentence in the rest of the statement?
Could the sentence appear in anyone's application?
Does it use the first person singular rather than the word we?
Does it contain a verb that shows a senior level of responsibility?

questions.prompt: Which rewrite best replaces 'embedded a culture of excellence'?

options.text: Introducing a monthly review where teams presented their most frequent errors, after which repeat errors fell
Ensuring that staff understood the importance of excellence through regular briefings and briefing packs for all grades
Leading a drive for excellence through the whole directorate and across its supplier chain in the department
Promoting a strong ethos of quality across the directorate and rewarding the teams that embodied it

questions.prompt: Why is 'significant savings' weaker than 'around a tenth of the annual running cost'?

options.text: The first is less formal and so less suited to a senior statement
The second is longer, and longer sentences always score higher
The first mentions money, which should not appear in statements
The second gives a defensible scale an assessor can weigh

questions.prompt: A candidate gives a figure they cannot explain. What risk does this create?

options.text: The figure will be ignored by assessors who cannot check it
The figure will reduce the word count available for the actions
The figure will help, because any number is better than none
They may be asked how it was calculated and be unable to defend it

questions.prompt: Which is a weakness of listing the whole portfolio an SEO manages?

options.text: It describes the job, not an action by the candidate
It is too short to cover the whole of the portfolio fairly
It shows too much responsibility for one example at this grade
It is not set out in the STAR format that the advert asks for

questions.prompt: Why avoid internal programme names and unexplained acronyms?

options.text: Assessors may be from another department and cannot score what they do not understand
They are not allowed in statements and are removed before scoring
They make the sentences long and so use up the word limit
They are unprofessional in a document that other people may read

questions.prompt: How do long chains of nouns and passive verbs affect a statement?

options.text: They hide who acted and make credit harder to give
They show seniority and a command of formal civil service writing
They shorten the statement and so leave more room for results
They increase accuracy, because they avoid personal opinion

questions.prompt: Which phrase is least informative?

options.text: Delivered at scale
Reduced the backlog from about 2,000 to 400 cases
Cut turnaround from ten days to six
Met the target for the third quarter running

questions.prompt: What should you do with a large portfolio when writing a single example?

options.text: Describe the whole portfolio in brief and then pick one example
Choose one or two moments and describe what you did
Cover each team in turn, with a line on what you did for it
Quote the organisation chart and the budget of each part of it

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the clearest?

options.text: The supplier landscape was optimised in a data-driven way across all of the contracts
I asked the three suppliers for monthly error data and stopped paying for rework
Supplier performance was enhanced through synergy between the commercial and delivery teams
A holistic review of suppliers took place and recommendations were made to the board

items.title: L12: How interviewers probe a senior example
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: A written statement is often followed by an interview in which the panel tests the same examples. At senior grades, probing is more searching, and a good preparation habit is to anticipate it. Panels commonly ask for the part you personally played, the alternatives you considered, what you would do differently, who disagreed with you and how you dealt with them, and how you knew the result was real. They may also ask what happened afterwards, because a change that did not last is weaker evidence than one that did. Expect questions that move the example sideways: 'What would you have done if the sponsor had refused?' tests judgement beyond the story. If your written account overclaimed, probing is where it is exposed, since answers that cannot name a date, a person or a figure sound thin. Equally, a candidate who gives detail that matches the statement, and who volunteers a difficulty, earns credibility. Prepare by re-reading every statement you submitted and listing, for each, the facts you could be asked about: the figures and how you reached them, the names of the groups involved, the timeline and your own decisions. Do not memorise a script; panels notice and may ask an unexpected follow-up that breaks it. If you do not know or do not remember a detail, say so plainly rather than guessing, and offer what you do know. Staying consistent also means not contradicting your statement: if something in it was imprecise, correct it calmly. Treat the probing as a chance to show depth, not as an accusation. Where the question concerns another Behaviour, answer honestly from the example if it fits, or briefly use a second example.

questions.prompt: Which question is a typical probe of a senior example?

options.text: Which of the Behaviours in the advert did you find hardest?
How would your current manager describe your work?
What was your own part, and what alternatives did you consider?
Which skills would you most like to develop in the new grade?

questions.hint: Panels test personal part and alternatives.

questions.prompt: Why might a panel ask what happened after the change?

options.text: Because the panel is checking that the example is recent enough
Because the panel wants to see how many colleagues the candidate can name
Because the panel has not yet read the written statement
A change that did not last is weaker evidence than one that did

questions.prompt: 'What would you have done if the sponsor had refused?' tests what?

options.text: Judgement beyond the story as told
How well the candidate gets on with the sponsor
Whether the sponsor would give the candidate a reference
How many meetings the candidate attended on the project

questions.prompt: Where is an overclaiming statement most likely to be exposed?

options.text: In the check of the statement's word count before sifting
In follow-up questions where the candidate cannot supply dates, people or figures
In the formatting and layout of the submitted document
In the order in which the paragraphs of the statement appear

questions.prompt: What is the best preparation habit for interview?

options.text: Memorise a script for each example and rehearse it word for word
Read other candidates' statements to see how they pitched theirs
Re-read each statement and list the facts you could be asked about
Learn the panel members' names and their areas of responsibility

questions.prompt: Why should a candidate avoid a memorised script?

options.text: Scripts are not allowed in interviews and are taken off candidates
Scripts take too long to deliver within the time the panel allows
Panels dislike structured answers and prefer informal conversation
Panels may ask an unexpected follow-up that breaks it

questions.prompt: A candidate cannot recall a figure from their statement. What is the best response?

options.text: Say so plainly and give what they do know
Give a figure that sounds right and is close to what you recall
Change the subject to another part of the example you remember well
Ask the panel to remind them of what the statement said

questions.prompt: Something in the statement was imprecise. What should the candidate do at interview?

options.text: Defend it as written, since changing it could look inconsistent
Avoid mentioning it unless the panel raises the point first
Ask for the question to be repeated and then move on to another point
Correct it calmly and explain the accurate position

questions.prompt: Which is a sign of credibility in an interview answer?

options.text: A very short answer that avoids saying anything that could be challenged
Repeating the question back before giving a general answer
A list of achievements from across the candidate's career
Detail that matches the statement and volunteering a difficulty

questions.prompt: The panel asks about a Behaviour your chosen example does not fit. What is the sensible approach?

options.text: Use the example if it genuinely fits, or briefly offer a second example
Give a general answer about the Behaviour with no example
Say that it was covered in the statement and ask to move on
Decline to answer because the example was not chosen for it
